drills.q: What happens to the realized false-positive rate if you repeatedly peek at a fixed-horizon test's p-value before its planned end?
drills.a: It inflates from the nominal ~5% to commonly cited estimates above 25% -- each look is effectively an additional implicit hypothesis test.

drills.q: What's the difference between the novelty effect and the primacy (change-aversion) effect?
drills.a: Novelty: users respond more positively simply because a variant is new -- a temporary false positive. Primacy/change aversion: users initially resist a genuinely better change out of habit -- a temporary false negative. Both decay as users adjust.

drills.q: Your test shows +8% lift on day 3 of a planned 14-day run, and leadership wants to ship immediately. What's wrong with calling this a win, and what would make it valid?
drills.a: This is the peeking problem -- an early significant-looking result on a fixed-horizon test doesn't control the false-positive rate at that interim point. It would only be valid with a pre-registered alpha-spending schedule or an always-valid/sequential testing method configured before the test started.

drills.q: A test on a SaaS product's core UI shows no significant difference. A stakeholder concludes the feature doesn't work. What's the correction?
drills.a: A null result only rules out effects larger than the achieved MDE at the sample size collected -- it says nothing about smaller real effects. Report the achieved MDE alongside the null result: 'we can rule out an effect larger than X%, but can't distinguish a smaller effect from none at this sample size.'

drills.q: Why would you keep a small holdback/control group running even after a variant has already 'won' and shipped to 100% of remaining traffic?
drills.a: To catch a lift that was partly or wholly novelty-driven and would fade over the following weeks -- comparing the holdback's stable long-run behavior to the shipped variant confirms whether the launch decision was actually correct, especially for high-stakes, hard-to-reverse changes.

drills.q: Why does a high-returning-traffic surface (e.g. a SaaS product UI) need a longer test runtime to trust results than a high-new-visitor landing page?
drills.a: Novelty/primacy effects require repeat exposure to manifest and decay. On a high-new-visitor surface most users see the change for the first time regardless of variant, so there's little differential; on a high-returning-traffic surface most of the treatment arm experiences a real change from habit, so the effect can be large and take weeks to wash out.

drills.q: A dashboard flags significance on one of fifteen tracked metrics for a test, none pre-registered as primary. How do you evaluate this and what do you recommend?
drills.a: This is multiple-metric fishing -- the same multiple-comparisons inflation as peeking, applied across metrics instead of time. Treat the result as directional/exploratory only, not a launch decision basis; if it's a genuinely important finding, run a new, focused test with that metric pre-registered as primary rather than retroactively promoting it.

drills.q: How would you concretely detect novelty/primacy decay in a running test rather than guessing an arbitrary extra runtime?
drills.a: Segment the analysis by new-vs-returning traffic and by exposure count within returning users (1st visit vs Nth visit post-launch). A flattening or reversing trend in lift as exposure count grows is the decay signature, and it tells you empirically when the effect has stabilized rather than picking a fixed calendar duration blindly.

drills.q: You have no dedicated experimentation platform and one week to add minimum guardrails before any team is allowed to make launch decisions off test results. What's the one thing you never cut, and what do you defer?
drills.a: Never cut the automated SRM check (chi-squared test on arm counts, hard-blocking the report) -- a few lines of code catching the most common invalidating bug. Defer the sequential-testing/always-valid tooling, replaced temporarily with the blunter 'lock the dashboard until planned sample size' rule, which costs nothing to implement and is still statistically safe, just less flexible.

drills.q: Explain why 'we use sequential testing' can be a hollow claim, and what you'd ask to verify it's real.
drills.a: A team can have the vocabulary without the protection -- eyeballing a live p-value chart with no alpha-spending schedule and no always-valid correction underneath is not sequential testing, it's uncorrected peeking with a label. Verify by asking what specific method is configured (which alpha-spending function, or which always-valid/mSPRT implementation) and whether it was set up before the test started, not retrofitted after someone noticed an early result.
